title: Neanderthals Were Adept Woodworkers Too - Nautilus
gist: Neanderthals had sophisticated stone and wooden toolkits, but most wooden tools have decayed. At Abric Romaní in Spain, travertine incrustation preserved impressions of wooden objects in cell-level detail, and a new Science Advances study examines this rare assemblage.

insights.claim: Contrary to the club-wielding caveman stereotype, Neanderthals made sophisticated stone tools including scrapers, axes, knives and even dentist drills.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A reminder that stereotypes can persist long after the evidence has moved on.
insights.quote: The traditional Neanderthal stereotype might be that of a club-wielding caveman, but they actually had some pretty sophisticated technology.

insights.claim: The surviving Neanderthal toolkit is biased toward stone because most wooden tools have decayed, so the archaeological record understates their technological range.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates survivorship bias: what is preserved is not the whole picture.
insights.quote: Most Neanderthal wooden tools have unfortunately been lost to the ravages of time—with a few exceptions.

insights.claim: Abric Romaní, a cliffside settlement in Spain occupied by Neanderthals around 70,000 to 39,000 years ago, holds evidence of wooden objects preserved by travertine incrustation.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Rare preservation sites give outsized insight into otherwise lost material culture.

insights.claim: In travertine incrustation, calcium carbonate builds up around wood that then decays, leaving an impression detailed enough to show individual plant cells; a new Science Advances study analyses such an assemblage.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Natural mineral casting enables study of perishable artefacts that would otherwise leave no trace.
